nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Decent work and economic growth|Economic stability|Economic resilience_qna_000
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What complicates the relationship between banks and economic resilience in the context of natural hazards?
nodes.answer: The relationship is complicated because banks can suffer losses and negative impacts that may limit their ability to provide recovery loans.
nodes.paragraph: Limiting the negative economic consequences of future natural hazard shocks is therefore an urgent and high-priority policy goal (Koubi, 2019; United Nations, 2015). It is widely acknowledged that the banking sector has an important role to play in this endeavour (Carney, 2015; Ranger et al., 2021; United Nations, 2023). By facilitating access to finance, banks can enhance economic resilience through critical times and contribute to sustained economic growth and employment participation across societal groups. This is particularly true for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and otherwise underserved and excluded populations, which are highly vulnerable to exogenous shocks. However, the relationship between natural hazards, banks, and real economic resilience is more complex than this. First, banks themselves can be negatively impacted and experience losses and threats to their financial health, potentially limiting the ability to supply recovery loans. Second, banks may differ in their willingness to support economic recovery based on their business models, ownership structures, and resulting objective functions (Beck et al., 2018; Brei & Schclarek, 2015).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Decent work and economic growth|Economic stability|Economic resilience_qna_001
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How does the resilience of the banking sector relate to the real economy's ability to withstand natural hazards?
nodes.answer: The resilience of the banking sector is a precondition for enhancing the resilience of the real economy to natural hazard shocks.
nodes.paragraph: Against this background, this review is motivated by the question of what a banking system looks like that best enhances the resilience of the real economy to natural hazard shocks, informing policy efforts to achieve sustained economic growth and employment in the face of worsening physical climate risks. Since the resilience of the banking sector itself is a precondition for this, the study is structured around two interrelated questions: First, what are the direct effects of natural hazard shocks on the banking system, in particular on bank stability, profitability, and credit supply? Second, how does the banking system shape the resilience of the real economy to natural hazard shocks? A burgeoning literature discusses the economic and financial consequences of climate change and natural hazard-related disasters. Previous reviews have assessed the impact of disasters on real economic development (Botzen et al., 2019; Lazzaroni & van Bergeijk, 2014), the role of insurance in the face of extreme weather events (Kousky, 2019; Lucas, Booth, & Garcia, 2021), the environmental and climate-related risk management practices of financial firms (Breitenstein et al., 2021), the impact of 49 How Banks are Impacted by and Mediate the Economic Consequences disasters on international financial flows, including foreign aid (Osberghaus, 2019; Zhou, Endendijk, & Botzen, 2023), the pricing of climate risks in financial assets and investor portfolios (Campiglio et al., 2022; Giglio et al., 2021; Monasterolo, 2020), and the implications of the transition to a low-carbon economy for financial stability, systemic financial risk, and financial regulation (D Orazio & Popoyan, 2019; Monasterolo, 2020; Semieniuk, Campiglio, Mercure, Volz, & Edwards, 2020).

nodes.question: What opportunity has the COVID-19 pandemic provided regarding economic principles?
nodes.answer: The COVID-19 pandemic has provided a unique opportunity for reflection and the potential for a collective reset to advance the principles of a wellbeing economy in a post-pandemic world.
nodes.paragraph: Economic prosperity and economic growth were also highly valued, as the third and fourth most important priorities, respectively. There are identifiable differences in how younger and older Australians prioritise a restored natural world, a life lived with dignity and economic prosperity. R. Milte et al. 1 Introduction In 2018, prior to the onset of the global COVID-19 pan - demic, governments from six developed countries (Scot - land, New Zealand, Iceland, Wales, Finland and Canada) combined to form the Wellbeing Economy Alliance (WEAII), an international network promoting a new way of economic thinking [1 ]. The WEAII rejects traditional economic indicators such as the maximisation of economic growth at any cost and instead aims to advance the key principles of a wellbeing economy; ensuring an equita- ble distribution of wealth and wellbeing, where caring is highly valued and where the planet S resources are pro- tected [1 4]. The advent of the global coronavirus dis- ease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has further exposed the cracks in the economic fabric of societies. In addition, it has provided a unique opportunity for reflection and the potential for a collective reset to advance the principles of a wellbeing economy in a post-pandemic world [3 ].

nodes.question: What are the two main concepts discussed in the paper related to energy shocks in the EU?
nodes.answer: The two main concepts are energy vulnerability and energy resilience, which are intertwined yet not overlapping concepts that address how economies cope with energy shocks.
nodes.paragraph: This is not surpris - ing, though. Energy is in fact one of the main drivers of the surge in inflation that, albeit attenuated, is still conditioning monetary policy and, hence, growth in most Received: 5 September 2024 / Revised: 10 February 2025 / Accepted: 11 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025Energy vulnerability and resilience in the EU: concepts, empirics and policy Dario Guarascio1 Jelena Reljic1 Francesco Zezza1,2 Francesco Zezza francesco.zezza@uniroma1.i 1 Department of Economics and Law, Sapienza University of Rome, Via del Castro Laurenziano, 9, 185 Rome, Italy 2 Levy Economics Institute of Bard College, 30 Campus Rd, NY 12504 Annandale-On-Hudson, USA 13 Journal of Industrial and Business Economicseconomies, including the European Union (EU) (Ferreira et al., 2024 ). To mitigate the risks of a renewed inflationary crisis, economic policy toolboxes are being updated in an effort to reduce vulnerabilities as well as strengthening resilience vis- -vis energy shocks. In the context of a generalized (and, yet, contradictory) rediscovery of industrial policy, the European Commission (EC) shifted from merely incentiv - lizing green consumption and investments, to interventions aimed at reinforcing not only renewable energy production, but also productive and technological capabilities in key supply chains (e.g., solar panels, batteries, wind turbines) (Kleimann et al., 2023 ; Veugelers et al., 2024 ).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Decent work and economic growth|Economic stability|Economic resilience_qna_004
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the two key concepts discussed in the paper regarding how economies cope with energy shocks?
nodes.answer: The two key concepts are energy vulnerability and energy resilience, which are intertwined yet not overlapping. They relate to the capacity of economies to minimize socio-economic costs and adjust post-shock based on their resources and structural characteristics.
nodes.paragraph: The two are intertwined yet not overlapping concepts (Stirling, 2014 ), as two entities facing the same degree of vulnerability vis-a-vis energy shocks for instance, because both have a large share of employees in energy intensive industries risking to lose their job should an energy shock occur might be heterogeneously endowed concerning the resources (e.g., relative diversification of the supplier base, ability to produce energy in house from renewable sources, technological-production capabilities in the green domain) needed to minimize socio-economic costs and accelerate post-shock adjustment. Both concepts, in turn, are linked to the dependence on specific energy sources, as well as the security of their supply. Indeed, resilience and vulnerability are multifaceted phenomena, assuming different shape and intensity according to the aspects that are emphasized (e.g., import dependency, geopolitical risks associated to the dependency on specific suppliers, degree of diversification of the energy portfo - lio) or the structural characteristics (e.g., sectoral specialization) of the entity (e.g., country, region, supply chain) taken into consideration. As a result, a proper assess - ment requires identifying the relevant determinants driving the phenomenon at stake, possibly grasping the relationships between them.
